    MARK FRIESENHAHN, INTERVENOR 579, ON BEHALF OF HIMSELF.


         Intervenor Mark Friesenhahn submits this Post-Hearing Brief.

         This Initial Brief identifies each of the issues in the Order of Referral and the Preliminary
Order. Where the Intervenor does comment, the comment is grounded in the unrebutted
engineering record. The applicants did not rebut the matters summarized below, and the applicants
waived cross-examination of Mr. Friesenhahn; those matters therefore stand unchallenged in the
evidentiary record.

I.INTRODUCTION
 I’m a 5th-gnerationTexan, live and work on my pecan farm in Comal County but also operate
 approximately 300 acres of ranch land in Menard and Schleicher Counties where routes for the
 proposed Bell County East to Big Hill 765-kV transmission line subject to this Brief are
 mapped near our ranch.



II.STATEMENT OF POSITION

 I respect that the Commission's statutory role is to select a route, not to redesign Texas's energy
 policy. However, PURA requires the Commission to determine whether the record supports
 the necessity and appropriateness of this specific project, and whether the proposed route
 satisfies the statutory requirements of least-impact routing, community values, environmental
 integrity, and landowner protection.

 I also understand that we (all of us Texans) have to make compromises to provide natural
 resources, infrastructure and other requirements to support our massive residential and

 Mark Friesenhahn Statement of position and Post-Hearing Brief, Control No 59475
                                                                      2
 commercial growth. I simply seek equitable and sensible solutions backed by sound
environmental, economic and business justification.

I res p ectful ly request t hat S OAH recomm end t hat t he P UCT paus e and re-
ev alu at e th e need for the proposed Bell County East to Big Hill 765-kV transmission line,
along with the other powerlines included in the Texas Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan
(STEP) report. These total $33 billion cost and burden over 70,000 acres of land for ROW. My
request is based on review and assessment of the demand forecast studies supporting the need for
the powerlines 1, review of the data, testimony and exhibits filed, the week-long hearing of the
evidence and cross- examinations, and post-hearing information filed to date.

With the plans and decision processes for the proposed powerlines progressing, I had to make a
choice:
   1. Option 1 - Remain silent and tacitly accept the applicant’s CCN amendment, or;
   2. Option 2 - Oppose routing of link R1, R2 and Q1, and state “these links will affect the
        beauty and wide-open nature of my ranch land,” –which they clearly will do based on
        my experience with a 345kV powerline on my Comal Pecan Farm and the massive
        amount of intervenor testimony and protest letters related to Docket 59475 – “so, put the
        powerline elsewhere”, or;
   3. Option 3 - Study the bases, demand forecasts and justification for the powerlines to
        convince myself that the powerlines are needed for the Permian Basin (PB) and that we
        are making the right business, environmental and land impact decisions. Decide that the
        needs determination for the powerlines is adequate.

Despite my concerns addressed with and inclination to pursue Option 2 above, I chose Option 3.
I believe we (all of us involved in the PUCT powerline projects) are rushing ahead to achieve
powerline completion deadlines while 1). factors underpinning the need for these powerlines are
changing rapidly and 2). the overall balance of power generation location and capacity, and
transmission location and capacity do not add up logically to provide the projected power
demands in the Permian Basin.

Numerous sources filed positions aligned with my pursuit of Option 3. 2 3 4 Of note is that 33
Texas House of Representative and 8 Senators filed an AMICI CURIAE in support of American
Stewards of Liberty motion to defer determination of need for the proposed 765-kV transmission
line projects. Included in the Amici Curiae is a study by the Texas Public Policy Foundation
arguing that Texas policymakers should pause implementation of ERCOT's 765-kV Strategic

   Transmission Expansion Plan (STEP) and consider alternatives to minimize the cost and impact
  of the future transmission buildout. (see footnotes).

  The following sections provide specific justification for my request.

III.DETERMNATION OF NEED

  Based on my assessment outlined in Option 3 above, I have concerns with the NEEDS
  DETERMINATION for the entire proposed 765 KV powerline plan that is based on ERCOT and
  other studies. These studies (cited in my footnotes) addressed HOW to move SOME of the
  forecast electric power west to the Permian Basin but did not include a full assessment of
  ADDITIONAL POWER GENERATION needed and WHERE IT NEEDS TO BE LOCATED,
  nor ALTERNATIVES to generate power on-site in the Permian Basin.

  Studies and Position Statements cited in the footnotes support my position that need for the
  powerlines has not been conclusively determined, nor has the question of where the power
  generation is coming from been answered.

  Simply stated, the applicants are proposing that WE PURCHASE A MULTI-BILLION $
  EXTENSION CORD WITHOUT A PLACE TO PLUG IT IN. A simple analogy is that you
  attach your weed eater to the expensive extension cord, but do not have an outlet to plug the
  extension cord into. The Applicant challenged my assessment of need (in rebuttal testimonies) 56,
  but sources in this brief and others have come to the same conclusion that I have:

  The MATERIAL BALANCE OF POWER-GENERATED, TRANSMISSION OF THAT
  POWER TO THE PB DEMAND AREA AND PB FORECAST DEMAND DOES NOT ADD
  UP, IS ILLOGICAL AND NEEDS TO BE REASSESSED.

  I am generally aware of the state statues & laws governing power generation and power
  transmission. The applicants are in the power transmission business that is regulated and
  guaranteed about a 10% rate of return on investment based on actual installed cost. It is
  noteworthy that numerous Intervenors estimate that the actual cost of STEP could be 2-3
  multiples of the conceptual $33 billion estimate. Power generation, on the other hand, is subject
  to free market conditions and demand.

  Demand in the PB is somewhat confusing given the amount or renewable power generation in
  place. Renewable energy power generation sources, including wind, solar and batteries appear to
  be adequate to meet demand if one looks only at installed capacity, BUT this power is
  unavailable for 30-40% of the time due to no sun at night and no wind weather conditions. The
  commercial industries require power 24/7/365. So, no matter how much renewable power is

the PB (and/or planned small modular nuclear reactors) will still be needed as a backup to the
renewable sources.

The business strategies and the projects necessary to efficiently satisfy a). the overall PB demand
forecast, b). needed power generation and where it is located, and c). the transmission of this
power to the PB are needed to understand the overall “picture” to make effective decisions. A
“Material Balance” (GW) for the PB to support strategic decisions was included in my Direct
Testimony 7 In summary, the material balance works out to the following:

       2.   PUCT Texas Energy Fund (TxEF) grants totaling about 8400 megawatts (8.4 GW).
      3.   Industry group data [such as the Environmental Integrity Project (EIP)] tabulated 130 natural gas power
           plant projects have been proposed in Texas, in part to help feed the artificial intelligence boom. The EIP
           inventory included proposed gas power plant projects that could cumulatively add over 58 gigawatts (GW)
           of new generating capacity to the state’s grid.
      4.   Taken together, the PUCT and industry estimates suggest a total of new generating capacity of perhaps 40-
           50 GW. About 2/3, or 35 GW (70%) of the generating capacity is planned for the eastern half of Texas.
           Maybe 15 GW is located in the west.


IV.FAILURE TO CONSIDER ALTERNATIVES 8

      During the hearing, several intervenors, myself included, questioned why Oncor did not
      evaluate generation-based alternatives, hybrid solutions, or upgrades to existing 345-kV
      corridors before proposing a new 765-kV greenfield route. In response to these questions,
      Mr.. Rasmusson, counsel for Oncor, stated on the record that Oncor is "in the transmission
      business, not the oil and gas business.''

      This statement is significant. It confirms that Oncor did not evaluate alternatives not because
      they were infeasible, but because they fell outside of Oncor's preferred business model.
      PURA does not allow a utility to avoid evaluating reasonable alternatives simply because
      they are not part of its corporate focus.

      PURA requires the Applicant to demonstrate that the proposed project is the least cost,
      least-impact solution. A utility cannot satisfy that burden by declining to evaluate alternatives
      because they fall outside its business model.




V.HEALTH AND SAFETY IMPACTS 9

      I personally sat through the cross-examination of Dr, Gelman , Applicants’ medical and
      health expert, during the hearings. He left several important concerns unanswered. The post-
      hearing brief of Loren & Charles Powell, Pro Se, on behalf of Oran Creek Ranch LLC
      succinctly summarize my concerns. A partial quote from their brief:

      “During the hearing, the Applicants' medical and health expert, Dr. Gelman, admitted that
      he had conducted no research whatsoever regarding EMF exposure or potential health
      impacts associated with 765-kV transmission lines. He further acknowledged that he was not

        familiar with peer-reviewed studies by other researchers that raise concerns about possible
       health effects from high-voltage transmission infrastructure.”

       I believe this cross-examination and numerous studies identified by Intervenors, but not
       considered by the Applicant, leave several significant health and safety concerns unanswered.

VI.QUESTIONS

  Why are the three east to west powerlines justified? They cost a lot and fall way short of
  satisfying the needs determination and in meeting the objective of delivering the power needed to
  improve the reliability of the Permian Basin power supply.

  Why not add adequate dispatchable power in the west, bypassing most of the proposed
  powerlines altogether?

  What are we missing in the “big picture”, considering that the applicant is proposing launch of
  the initial parts of a $33 billion project, that once “launched” will be difficult to stop?

  What health impacts may be identified with a more thorough evaluation of EMF data from 765
  kV powerlines?

VII.CONCLUSION AND RELIEF REQUESTED

  With the major and long-reaching concerns and omissions in required statuary work by the
  applicant outlined above, I respectfully request SOAH recommend that PUCT pause the existing
  CCN amendment review work and reassess the overall STEP plan. Specifically, I request that the
  PUCT, with direction, backing and support by the Texas legislature, the Texas Water
  Development Board (TWDB) and other agencies as appropriate, implement the following
  recommendations 10:

       •   Pause the ERCOT/PUCT’s plans and order reassessment, given the questionable need for
           and utility rate cost impacts of these powerlines. A reassessment of the whole project is
           needed.
       •   Direct ERCOT to reassess the overall forecasts that led to justification for the powerlines.
           I cite a number of significant reasons for this in my filed Direct Testimony.
       •   Work with the legislature to Direct State agencies, including the TCEQ and TWDB, to
           revise permit strategies for AI data, Bit Coin mining centers, silicon crystal and chip
           manufacturing and other industries that consume large amounts of power and water. Do
           not provide power through infrastructure provided by rate payers. Require on-site power
           generation for these large corporations, with design criteria that addresses deficiencies in
           the existing PB power transmission system.


   Summarized from pgs. 10-12 of Control Number - 59475 Item Number – 4542, DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
  10

  MARK J. FRIESENHAHN

  Mark Friesenhahn Statement of position and Post-Hearing Brief, Control No 59475
                                                           7
      •   Include a complete and public review of the current science of health and environmental
         impacts of 765 kV powerlines, including Electromagnetic Field (EMF) exposure. There
         are many studies on the topic; fewer on 765 kV powerlines, and findings have historically
         been mixed. During the hearing, the Applicants' medical and health expert, Dr. Gelman,
         admitted that he had conducted no research whatsoever regarding EMF exposure or
         potential health impacts associated with 765-kV transmission lines. He further
         acknowledged that he was not familiar with peer-reviewed studies by other researchers
         that raise concerns about possible health effects from high-voltage transmission
         infrastructure 11.
     •   We realize that forecasting and providing new infrastructure to support rapidly growing
         and changing commercial developments across Texas is challenging to say the least.
         We’re shooting at a target that is moving very fast. It’s possible that we’ll ultimately
         need a reasonable combination of power generation and transmission powerlines to meet
         all needs. If a thorough reassessment of power demands requires one or more powerlines
         to serve the PB are ultimately needed:
         o Evaluate High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) as an alternative, especially given the
             400 mi +/ distances involved that favor HVDC.
         o Order a thorough review and application of obligatory Best Management Practices
             (BMPs) to minimize the impact on the environment, nearby landowners, and property
             values.

IV.FAILURE TO CONSIDER ALTERNATIVES 8

      During the hearing, several intervenors, myself included, questioned why Oncor did not
      evaluate generation-based alternatives, hybrid solutions, or upgrades to existing 345-kV
      corridors before proposing a new 765-kV greenfield route. In response to these questions,
      Mr.. Rasmusson, counsel for Oncor, stated on the record that Oncor is "in the transmission
      business, not the oil and gas business."

      This statement is significant. It confirms that Oncor did not evaluate alternatives not because
      they were infeasible, but because they fell outside of Oncor's preferred business model.
      PURA does not allow a utility to avoid evaluating reasonable alternatives simply because
      they are not part of its corporate focus.

      PURA requires the Applicant to demonstrate that the proposed proj ect is the least cost,
      least-impact solution. A utility cannot satisfy that burden by declining to evaluate alternatives
      because they fall outside its business model.
